name: allox (Rust general-purpose allocator)
baseline: glibc malloc (the 'system' column of the Linux table), mimalloc and snmalloc, each driven through a Rust GlobalAlloc wrapper; Rust-native talc and dlmalloc are also compared
workload: 22 allocator workloads run through GlobalAlloc: small, mixed and large size classes, 1 and 8 threads, zeroed allocation, producer/consumer remote free, thread churn, realloc growth; ops/s, higher is better.
claimed_speedup: Linux x86-64 (Ryzen 5 1600) table, ops/s: tight-small 1T 52.52 M/s vs glibc system 44.77, mimalloc 48.00, snmalloc 41.54 (1.09x vs best); mixed-small 8T 196.03 M/s vs system 37.17, mimalloc 40.42, snmalloc 57.87 (3.39x vs best); large-only 1T (32 K-1 M) 7.36 M/s vs system 340 K/s, mimalloc 2.52 M/s (2.91x vs best); big-upper-tail 1T 6.28x vs best. README: '21/22 win-or-tie against the best comparator'; the one real loss is zeroed-small 8T at 0.67x (snmalloc about 149 M/s vs allox 100.45 M/s). Windows table: 5/5 wins, 3.70x to 23.8x vs the system allocator.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench (Rust, MSRV 1.79); rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated. Comparator crates mimalloc, snmalloc, talc and jemalloc are dev-dependencies built with their crate defaults.
hardware: Linux x86-64 AMD Ryzen 5 1600, taskset -c 0-7, 3 GiB cgroup, BENCH_FRESH=1 BENCH_SAFE_LIVE=1, one fresh process per allocator/workload/repetition, median of 3 x 2 s runs. The Windows x86-64 table names no CPU.
why_faster: README: every fast path is lock-free per thread with sharded class locks touched only by batched slow paths, while single-heap allocators (talc, dlmalloc) serialize on one mutex; no mechanism is given for the glibc/mimalloc/snmalloc gaps on the mixed-size and large rows.
tradeoffs: Rust crate with a GlobalAlloc type and allox::malloc/free functions; peak RSS is higher on several rows (93 MiB mixed-small 8T, 118 MiB mixed-all 8T, 300 MiB prodcons 8T). Loses to snmalloc and mimalloc on 8-thread zeroed small allocations.
caveats: Very young single-author repo (1 star). Workloads are the author's own; rows carry a stated ~10% noise floor; mimalloc/snmalloc are measured through Rust wrappers, not LD_PRELOAD in a C program; glibc and C compiler versions unstated; no independent reproduction. The README documents a failed explanation hunt for the one loss rather than hiding it.

name: sefer-alloc (SeferAlloc, Rust allocator with large-segment cache)
baseline: mimalloc (C, via the Rust mimalloc 0.1 crate as GlobalAlloc) and the Windows System allocator
workload: criterion micro-benchmarks calling SeferAlloc directly through GlobalAlloc: alloc(N)+free round trips of 4, 16 and 64 MiB served by a large-segment cache, realloc growth chains, small-size churn and cold-path tables.
claimed_speedup: README large alloc/free table (lower is better): 4 MiB ~58.6 ns vs mimalloc ~716 ns (~12.2x) vs System ~17.7 us (~302x); 16 MiB ~61.9 ns vs ~1.13 us (~13.5x); 64 MiB ~60.8 ns vs ~2.58 us (~33x). realloc_grow_geometric (64 B to 4 MiB) ~238 us vs mimalloc ~431 us (~1.8x); realloc_grow_neighbour_pressure ~400 ns vs ~1.34 ms (~3,350x). About text: 'Up to ~18x faster than mimalloc on cached large alloc/free'. README also states 0.3.0 loses to mimalloc on the cold path at 16-64 B (~1.9-2.7x slower).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --features production (criterion, sample_size(10), short warm-up); rustc version and flags not stated; mimalloc is the mimalloc 0.1 crate used as a dev-dependency baseline.
hardware: A single Windows dev host, CPU model not stated; README gives host noise as +-15-20 percent.
why_faster: README: the OPT-E large-segment cache keeps pages committed so a same-size re-allocation returns without an OS round trip, while mimalloc and System go back to the OS.
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no libnuma/mimalloc/jemalloc dependency; handle store plus global allocator. README discloses a Miri-reported undefined-behaviour case (P1-box: free-list links inside freed small blocks) and a MAX_SEGMENTS pinning limit for long-running processes with many small-segment cycles.
caveats: Headline ratios hold only for same-size reuse inside the decay window with a size factor of 2x or less; README says not to extrapolate to mixed-size or cold first-touch workloads. Single Windows host with unstated CPU, quick bench profile, and some 16/64 MiB mimalloc/System absolute cells are carried from an earlier run. The exact '~18x' figure was not found in the README tables (12x-33x are). Sole author, 1 star.

name: tac (neosmart, SIMD-accelerated Rust rewrite of GNU tac)
workload: Reversing the lines of a file (tac FILE); README gives no input size or command.
claimed_speedup: README: 'significantly (2.55x if mitigations disabled, more otherwise) faster than the version of tac that ships with GNU Coreutils'.
why_faster: README: AVX2/NEON SIMD newline detection plus memory-mapped input, which avoids read-syscall cost when speculative-execution mitigations are enabled.
tradeoffs: Fast path needs a seekable file; stdin is buffered in memory up to 4 MiB then spilled to disk, so piped input loses the advantage. NEON needs the nightly compiler.
caveats: One number with no hardware, GNU tac version, input or command; no benchmark script in the repo's top level; the author's blog post (neosmart.net) was not opened because blogs are blocked here. Last release 2.1.0 in January 2024.

name: crabz (Rust pigz-style compressor on gzp, pure-Rust deflate backend)
workload: Parallel gzip compression at levels 3, 6, 9 with 1 to 32 threads, and gzip decompression, of the bench-data text catted together 100 times, timed with hyperfine.
claimed_speedup: README takeaways: crabz with the rust backend is roughly 5-10% faster than pigz (zlib backend identical, zlib-ng backend 30-50% faster). Rust-backend table (mean seconds): level 3, 1 thread 10.167 vs pigz 11.338 (1.11x, derived from page data); level 3, 32 threads 0.547 vs 0.755 (1.38x); level 9, 1 thread 44.907 vs 53.109 (1.18x); level 9, 32 threads 1.747 vs 2.086 (1.19x); level 6 is a tie (27.064 vs 27.034 at 1 thread, 1.192 vs 1.196 at 32). Decompression 1.599-1.615 s vs pigz 1.696-1.767 s (1.06-1.11x).
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release --no-default-features --features deflate_rust,libdeflate,snap_default (benchmark.sh); rustc version for the original run not stated (repo now pins 1.97.1); pigz is the distro binary with unstated flags. hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 3.
hardware: Ubuntu 20, AMD Ryzen 9 3950X 16-core, 64 GB DDR4, 1 TB NVMe
tradeoffs: The zlib-ng and libdeflate backends are C libraries; only the deflate_rust backend (miniz_oxide) is pure Rust. Level numbers of miniz_oxide and zlib do not mean the same compression effort.
caveats: README does not report compressed sizes, so a faster deflate_rust run may simply produce larger output; the README itself says 'none of this is groundbreaking' because zlib-ng is known to beat zlib. Numbers are from the Ubuntu 20 era with pigz 2.4. benchmark.sh is public, so this is close to tier A except for the missing rustc version and distro-built baseline.

name: qj (jq 1.8.1 ported to Rust, simdjson via FFI)
baseline: jq (C; version not stated in the benchmark, qj is a port of jq 1.8.1)
workload: jq filters over a 3.4 GB GitHub Archive NDJSON file (1.2M records) and a 49 MB single JSON file, file input unless noted.
claimed_speedup: README, M5 Max MacBook Pro, hyperfine: NDJSON .actor.login 144 ms (parallel) / 1.32 s (1 thread) vs jq 18.0 s, jaq 6.7 s, gojq 17.2 s; select(.type == "PushEvent") 163 ms / 1.68 s vs jq 32.2 s (198x); {type,repo,actor} 152 ms / 1.46 s vs jq 19.8 s. 49 MB JSON '.statuses | map({user, text})' 35 ms vs jq 646 ms (18x); 5-28x on single files; stdin ~15-29x; slurp mode ~5-6x. Single-thread .actor.login is 13.6x over jq (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo [profile.release] opt-level = 3, lto = "thin", edition 2024; jq build/version and rustc version not stated; simdjson (C++) is vendored and called via FFI.
why_faster: README: SIMD parsing (simdjson), mmap, automatic parallelism across cores, and direct evaluation of simple filters on simdjson's tape; the single-thread row isolates most of the non-parallel part.
tradeoffs: Memory: ~80-410 MB sliding window on the 3.4 GB file vs jq's ~6 MB. Core is Rust but the parser is C++ simdjson through FFI, so it is not pure Rust. Gains shrink for stdin and slurp.
caveats: Most of the 198x is parallelism plus mmap plus the simple-filter shortcut on a large NDJSON file; single-file gains are 5-28x. Benchmark scripts live in benches/ (not opened); jq version and build unstated. Young repo with a large commit count. Also listed as a parked cross-wave lead in QUEUE.md.

name: minifind (dkorunic, Rust parallel find(1) reimplementation)
workload: Walking a shallow clone of the mainline Linux kernel tree (100,871 entries in 6,201 directories, ~2.1 GB) with a warm page cache; both tools run as subprocesses with output discarded; 100 Criterion samples.
claimed_speedup: README: minifind 26.634-26.779 ms (26.702 ms point) vs find 92.463-93.565 ms (93.0 ms), about 3.5x faster (3.8M vs 1.1M entries/s).
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench walk (Criterion, benches/walk.rs); rustc version, profile flags and GNU find version not stated.
hardware: 4-core / 8-thread Intel Xeon E5-1630 v3 @ 3.70 GHz, 48 GB RAM
why_faster: README: parallel work-stealing traversal (most of the gap on 8 threads), raw getdents64 via rustix, d_type instead of a per-entry stat, batched output thread with a 256 KB writer, mimalloc.
tradeoffs: Supports a subset of find(1) options. Uses mimalloc. README says the advantage scales with core count and shrinks toward parity on 1-2 core hosts and on a cold cache.
caveats: Win is mostly parallelism against single-threaded GNU find; process startup is included for both. Benchmark code is public but compiler/profile and GNU find version are not stated, so it falls just short of tier A. Repo contains AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files (AI-assisted development).

name: tachyon-rs (Rust SIMD AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, MD5, SHA, BLAKE3, Base64)
baseline: OpenSSL libcrypto (C and assembly; versions 3.2.1 to 3.6.1 depending on platform) for AES-128-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305 and MD5; ring 0.17.14 and the blake3 1.8.2 crate are also compared
workload: Single-call throughput on 64 KiB buffers (AES-128-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 encryption, MD5, SHA-1, BLAKE3) and 192 KiB Base64 encoding, MiB/s, on up to eleven x86-64 and ARM platforms.
claimed_speedup: AES-128-GCM 64 KiB, tachyon vs OpenSSL: Apple M4 12212 vs 11043; M1 8411 vs 8143; A16 9225 vs 7330; Snapdragon 888 4759 vs 3972; RPi4 BCM2711 56.4 vs 23.4; Ryzen Z1 Extreme 18458 vs 16407; Ryzen 9 9950X 33179 vs 33121 (tie). ChaCha20-Poly1305: Ryzen 9 9950X 7576 vs OpenSSL 6900 vs ring 3714; Apple M4 2855 (tune-cpu=generic build) vs 2356, but 1730 with the default build; i7-3770 1122 vs 1106 while ring is 1151. MD5 beats OpenSSL on 9 of 10 platforms (e.g. Ryzen 9 9950X 1289 vs 1187), loses on Apple M4 (966 vs 982). BLAKE3 beats the blake3 crate on Apple and Snapdragon (M4 3459 vs 2572) and loses on x86 (Ryzen 9 9950X 13348 vs 13441).
compiler_and_flags: Rust, benchmarks in bench/; no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu given except nightly -Ztune-cpu=generic for some ARM rows; OpenSSL build options not stated.
hardware: Apple M4, M1, A16, A12z; Snapdragon 888 and 6 Gen 1; BCM2711 (RPi4); Intel i7-10700K and i7-3770; AMD Ryzen 9 9950X and Ryzen Z1 Extreme
why_faster: README claims hand-tuned SIMD intrinsics (AVX/SSE, NEON) 'outperform even hand-tuned assembly in many cases'; no per-primitive mechanism is given.
tradeoffs: README security notice: not formally audited, for benchmarking and experimentation, do not use in production. Pure Rust (no C), x86-64 and aarch64 only.
caveats: Wins are mostly on ARM and Apple chips where OpenSSL's code is weaker; on x86 it ties or loses (AES-GCM Ryzen 9 9950X tie, BLAKE3 slower, ChaCha20 on i7-3770 behind ring). OpenSSL versions differ per platform, so rows are not a single controlled comparison. Hand-written assembly baselines are not compared directly except through OpenSSL. First-party tables only.
